explain.say: When you hold a ball up, it has stored energy from its height. As it falls, that turns into movement energy, and when it hits the floor the ball squashes like a spring.

explain.say: The squashed ball springs back into shape and pushes off the floor, turning its stored springy energy back into upward movement.

explain.say: But no ball is a perfect spring. Some energy warms the rubber as it squashes, and some leaves as the thud you hear, so less is left to lift the ball.

explain.say: Each bounce keeps about the same fraction of the energy, so the heights shrink step by step, say from 1 metre to 70 centimetres, then to 49, until the ball comes to rest.

faq.q: Why does a ball bounce at all?
faq.a: When it hits the ground the ball squashes and stores energy like a compressed spring. As it springs back to its round shape it pushes against the floor, and the floor pushes it back up.

faq.q: Where does the lost energy go?
faq.a: Most of it becomes heat. The rubber rubs inside itself as it squashes and springs back, warming slightly, and a little energy leaves as sound and as a push on the floor.
asks: Why does a ball warm up when it bounces?

faq.q: Why do some balls bounce higher than others?
faq.a: Balls made of very springy material, like a solid rubber superball, give back most of their energy, while a lump of clay gives back almost none. Air pressure matters too: a flat football bounces poorly.
asks: Why does a superball bounce so high?

faq.q: Why does a ball bounce lower on sand?
faq.a: Soft ground like grass or sand squashes too and soaks up the energy instead of springing it back. A hard floor returns more energy to the ball.
asks: Why don't balls bounce on sand?

faq.q: Can a ball bounce higher than where it was dropped?
faq.a: Not on its own, because it would need more energy than it started with. It can only go higher if you throw it down, giving it extra energy.
asks: Can a ball bounce back higher?

facts: Energy is never destroyed; in a bouncing ball it gradually changes into heat and sound.
Official tennis balls are tested by dropping them from 254 centimetres; they must bounce back to between about 135 and 147 centimetres on a hard surface.
